The session begins.

The Trade Way ends in noise. Carts grind onto the stones of Wyrm's Crossing, porters shout over each other, and somewhere above the river a bell marks the evening. Lamps are being lit one by one along the bridge. Houses and shopfronts lean over the span, so the crossing feels less like a road and more like a narrow, crowded street hanging over the Chionthar.

The queue at the checkpoint shuffles forward. A family with bundles on their backs passes the trestle table; a carter argues about a toll and loses. Behind the table, a Flaming Fist sergeant with ink on her fingers and a chipped red gauntlet rubs her eyes and writes on a chalkboard without looking up much.

A few paces off the line, a lean man in a too-good waistcoat has turned a barrel into a table. Three cards flick under his hands, face down, face up, face down. "Find the lady, friends, find the lady! Long road, short game, a silver says you've still got your eye!" A couple of waiting drovers lean in to watch. The cards slap down again, crisp and familiar.

At James's feet, the cat has stopped. Its tail is up and its ears are turned, not toward the cards, but somewhere along the bridge, where the lamplight thins between two shuttered stalls.

The man in front of James steps up to the table. The sergeant's chalk taps the board.

"Next after this one — name, and your business in the Gate."

James keeps his eyes on the trestle. The cards are still slapping down behind him, *find the lady, friends*, and he doesn't look. Under his fingers the cat's ears flatten for a moment, then come back up. It doesn't move from his boot.

The answer comes the way the cat's answers always come, more feeling than words: *Still there. Not moving. Watching the barrel-man. Not us.*

The sergeant glances at the pay slip, then looks at it properly. She turns it a little toward the lamp with one inky finger, and the Tethyrian seal catches the light.

"Zaranda's." She doesn't say it like a compliment, but she doesn't say it like an insult either. She chalks *WORGEN* onto the board in square capitals, then copies it into a thick ledger lying open by her elbow. Her pen moves along the page past the day's names. A few lines higher up, two or three names carry a small chalk cross in the margin, done in the same hand.

"Business, work," she says as she writes. She looks at the cat once, briefly. "The cat's not my problem till it bites someone. Walking's free. Carts pay."

She slides the pay slip back across the trestle.

"A bed. Inside the walls, the Elfsong. It's dear, but nobody wakes up short there. Out here—" she tips her head north along the span, toward the lamps and the dark bulk of Wyrm's Rock in the middle of the river "—Tallow's, last door before the Rock. A widow runs it. She bars the door at midnight and counts the spoons. Her prices will rob you. Nobody else will."

The chalk taps once against the board while she thinks about something.

"Honest work, the Fist is hiring. It pays late. But it pays."

Then she looks past his shoulder, at the barrel and the lean man's busy hands, and her mouth goes flat.

"And whatever you do in the Gate, don't win anything at that barrel." She has already turned to the family behind him. "Next. Name, and your business."

James leans on the lamp post and lets his shoulders drop like a man who has walked a long way and hasn't decided where to sleep. The cat leaves his boot without any fuss. It pads to the nearest stall, goes up a rain barrel and onto the low shingled roof, and is gone along the ridge line, just a darker shape against the dark.

That leaves James with the barrel.

The man in the waistcoat is good. He isn't great, but he's good, and on a bridge at dusk that's plenty. It's the old throw. He holds two cards in his right hand, one above the other, and lets one fall. Every eye on the barrel follows the top card down. Every time, the card that drops is the bottom one. His patter rides over it: *watch her, friend, watch the lady, she's shy*. The drovers follow the card they think they saw, and they lose a silver each, cheerfully, one after another. Nobody beats that throw by watching. You'd have to stop his hand.

Then he does something James doesn't expect.

A broad drover in a sheepskin puts down his silver. The waistcoat man slows down, only a hair. The lady's corner has a crimp in it, and for one pass he lets it show, the way a sharp gives a win to his shill so the crowd will play. But the drover isn't a shill. He's a stranger with dung on his boots, and he points straight at the lady and turns her over and whoops.

"There she is, there she is! You've got the eye, friend." The sharp gives back the silver stake. Then he doesn't go into the waistcoat pocket where the rest of the evening's silver went. He opens a second purse, small and greasy, tied apart on his left hip, and counts coppers out of it into the drover's palm. Ten of them. "Copper spends the same, friend, copper spends the same."

The drover grumbles about it, laughing, and pockets them. The sharp pulls the purse string tight and settles it back on his hip with a little pat, the way you'd check a knife you don't want to cut yourself on. The next man in loses two silver straight, and all of that goes into the waistcoat.

A thin boy in a too-big jacket has been hovering at the back of the drovers. He edges forward with a coin pinched in his fingers. The sharp doesn't even look up. "Not tonight, little friend. You've had yours this week." The boy hangs there a moment, then slides off into the crowd going south.

The cat's answer reaches James before the cat does, the way it always does: cold slate under its paws, then a picture behind his eyes.

*One. Man. Sitting on a crate in the gap, back to the wall. Grey coat, hood down. Young. Smells of ale and onions.* Then, sharper: *Steel. Short. Left side of his belt.* And then something the cat clearly finds odd: *He scratches a stick with the knife. Each time the barrel-man takes silver, a scratch. When the barrel-man paid, no scratch. He looked at the purse. Long look.*

The cat comes down the rain barrel and settles against James's boot again as if it had never gone. The drover in the sheepskin is shoving through toward the lamps, jingling his winnings, and as he passes the post every hair along the cat's spine stands up.

*Smell,* the cat sends, flat and urgent. *On him. Wet stone. Old candles. Wrong.* It watches the sheepskin coat go off north along the span until the crowd swallows it.

The man in the gap hasn't moved. The sharp has already started his patter for the next mark. The checkpoint queue shuffles forward, and nobody is looking at a tired traveller leaning on a lamp post.

James lets the patter fade behind him: *watch the lady, friend, she's shy*. The lamp post gives him up without fuss, and he's just another tired back with a pack on it, walking north where the sergeant pointed.

The cat goes up a drainpipe and is gone. A moment later the feeling of it comes back: tar-paper and wet shingles under its paws, the drop to the street on one side, and threaded through the bridge's smells of fish, smoke, horse and too many people, one cold line of *wet stone, old candles*, moving north at a walk.

Following him is easy. The drover isn't hiding from anyone. He's a big man in a big coat, pleased with himself, and he walks the way a countryman walks in a town, down the middle of the street, stopping to look at things. A handcart of turnips is going the same way. James drifts in behind it and lets its owner set the pace, about forty-five feet back. His boots make no sound on the stones. The houses lean in overhead. Upstairs a woman is shaking out a cloth from a window, someone is frying onions, and a child somewhere is being told off for the third time.

Halfway along the span the drover stops at a pie-man's brazier. He buys a hot mutton pie and pays with a silver bit from his own coat. The coppers stay where they are, and he gives the pocket a pat and a jingle as if they might be lonely. The pie-man makes change. The drover turns away with the pie in his fist and his mouth already open for it.

His bootlace snaps.

James sees it happen. The man puts his weight on his right foot, the boot slides half off his heel, and he goes down on one knee in the gutter. The pie lands face-first in something that came out of a horse. The drover kneels there and looks at it. Then he laughs, a big, rueful laugh, and the pie-man laughs with him and won't give him another for free. The drover gets up, wet to the knee, ties the broken lace in a fat knot, and goes on north with his boot flapping.

*Same smell,* the cat sends from somewhere above. *Stronger when he fell. Like a cellar door opened.* Then, uneasy, it adds: *Fur wants to go up. I don't let it.*

The drover doesn't go down to the water and doesn't meet anyone on the street. Near the north end of the span, where the bulk of Wyrm's Rock fills the sky and the houses give way to the old fortress wall, he ducks under a low lintel into a taproom built right out over the railing. A sign hangs by one chain: a painted fence rail and six copper pennies, *The Sixpenny Rail*. Through the open door come lamplight, pipe smoke, and the noise of a room full of drovers and carters. A cheer goes up for him, someone shouts *what happened to you, then?*, and he starts telling it.

Three doors further on, the last door before the Rock, a narrow house shows a single lit window and a brass plate polished to a shine. That's Tallow's. Its door is open for now, with midnight still hours off.

The cat settles on the Rail's roof ridge, right above the door, and tucks its paws under. *He sits. By the fire. Others round him. The smell stays with him.*

Nothing else on the street is paying any attention to James. The turnip cart rattles on toward the fortress gate without him.

The cat following a scent along the roofs is ordinary for it too. They all succeeded as written: the drover never spotted James, he didn't turn off the bridge, go down to the water or meet anyone on the way, and the cat kept him in its nose all the way to the Sixpenny Rail.)*

The Sixpenny Rail is one long low room. Its back wall is the bridge railing itself, boarded in and shuttered against the river. There's a fire at one end and a plank bar at the other, and in between is a fug of pipe smoke, wet wool and boiled mutton. Somebody has hung a horse collar over the hearth for luck.

A stout woman with her sleeves pushed up looks at the silver, decides it's real, and sweeps it into her apron. A tankard of something brown arrives. Then comes a wooden bowl of mutton and barley with a heel of bread stuck upright in it. The silver covers both, and she doesn't offer change and doesn't seem to expect to be asked for any.

James turns on the stool with his back to the bar and the tankard in his hand.

The drover tells it well. He was born to it. The lace goes *snap*, the pie goes face-down in the muck, and the pie-man's face gets worse each time it comes round, until the carters by the fire are wiping their eyes. He's maybe forty, red-faced, with forearms like hams. Every time he gets to the part where he still had his winnings, he slaps the pocket of the sheepskin and it chinks.

Each time it chinks, the coin under James's shirt goes cool.

It isn't cold to the skin, and nothing anyone could see. It feels like a draught where a door has opened in another room. It happens with the first chink, again with the second, and again with the third. Between the slaps it warms back to his own heat.

Then James raises his tankard toward the fire and the whole corner turns to look.

"Keeps fine, friend!" The drover slaps the pocket again, and the coin goes cool again. "Keeps right here. Bram Tolley never lost a penny he'd won fair. Forty head up from Beregost and not one gone lame, and now the lady's own luck on top." He lifts his tankard back at James. The handle turns in his wet fist, and half a pint goes down the front of the sheepskin.

The corner roars. Bram looks down at himself, dripping, and laughs the loudest of anyone.

"*That's* barrel-luck, is it? Here, then." He digs into the pocket and comes out with a copper between two thick fingers. It's a worn, dark little penny. "Lady's own penny. Call it, stranger. Heads, and Bram stands you the next."

He doesn't wait for a call. He flips it with his thumb, high and showy. It comes down on the edge of the table, hops off, and rolls. It goes under one stool and between a carter's boots, and runs on across the floorboards in a long, wobbling curve as though the floor slopes toward the bar, though nothing else in the room has rolled that way. It ticks against the side of James's pack, between his feet, and lies down flat.

Under his shirt, Tymora's coin goes cold. It's a real cold this time, the kind he'd feel through cloth.

"Ah, *curse* it." Bram is half out of his seat, ale-soaked and grinning, with one hand out. "Throw that back, would you, friend? That's a tenth of my fortune you're standing on."

Close up, the penny is a worn thing, rubbed nearly smooth. There's the ghost of a ship's prow on the face, so it's probably a Gate penny, struck a long time ago. On the rim, where no moneyer puts anything, a tiny dark mark has been pressed into the copper. It wasn't scratched in. It's branched, like a forked twig or a stag's horn, and so small he has to turn it twice to be sure it's there. James has seen clipped edges, shaved coins, a cheat's notch in a marked deck. This is none of those, and he can't place it. It sits there on the rim and keeps its meaning to itself.

He sits up, already making the switch. As his palm closes, something warm brushes the nape of his neck, like a breath, and is gone. It doesn't help. His own copper goes out in a nice easy arc and smacks into Bram's wet fist. The cuff pulls back a hair too far on the flick, and his fingers fold the dark penny in a half-beat late.

"Tails, friend. Lady's luck says I buy my own. Keep your fortune."

Bram laughs and opens his hand to look. Then he stops laughing and turns the coin over. It's a bright copper with a sharp face, a Tethyrian penny from somewhere south of Amn.

"Hold up." He holds it toward the fire. "That's not her. Mine's dark as a cowpat and smooth as a baby's backside. This one's still got a king on it." The nearest carters are looking now: first at the coin, then at James's cuffed hand in his lap. Somebody by the hearth goes *ohhh* in the way men do when a joke might be about to become something else.

Bram is still grinning, but his eyes have stopped joining in. He leans forward on his stool with the bright penny held up between two fingers.

"Quick hands for a tired man. Where's my penny, then?"

Bram looks at them for a long moment. He's no longer grinning, and nothing else in the room is moving either.

Then he reaches past the silver and picks the dark penny out of James's linen with his bare, thick fingers.

"No, friend." He doesn't say it angrily, but he says it firmly. "Forty head up the Way and none of 'em lame. I've been unlucky before. A lace is a lace and a pie's a pie, and I spilled my ale because I'm a great clumsy ox, ask anyone here." Somebody does laugh at that, but only a little. "I won her fair. If I sell her for a silver to the first quick-handed stranger who tells me she's cursed, then I didn't win her, did I? I just got paid to carry her up the bridge for you."

He drops the penny into the sheepskin pocket and slaps it once, out of habit. Under James's shirt, Tymora's coin goes cool and stays that way.

He pushes the silver back across the table with one finger and leaves it lying by James's hand. Then he flicks the bright Tethyrian penny after it. It spins, falls flat, king up.

"And there's your king. Bram Tolley doesn't keep what isn't his, either." He looks at James a beat longer, and some of the earlier warmth comes back into his face, though not all of it. "But you owned up, I'll give you that. Most wouldn't have."

He turns back to the fire and the corner closes round him. Someone starts on a story about a mule.

It isn't quite over, though. An old carter in a leather cap is sitting at the end of the bench, and he didn't laugh at any of it. He leans over to Bram without looking at James and speaks low. He isn't quite low enough.

"You spend them coppers before you sleep, Bram. Humour me." He sucks his pipe. "And keep off the quays while you're in the Gate. You've heard what the Fist keeps fishing out down there. Men with a coin in their teeth."

"Umberlee's tithe," Bram says, and snorts. "I'm a drover, Ned. The sea can whistle for me." But he doesn't slap the pocket again.

The barkeep sets down a refilled jug of something for the fire corner and gives James one flat look, the sort a woman gives a man she hasn't decided about yet. On the roof the cat shifts its weight. *Street is quiet. No grey coat. Smell is still inside, under me.*

Your mutton is going cold beside the silver and the king-faced penny.

 James's offer doesn't move him. The honest owning-up and the silver on the table come up a hair short against the drover's pride, so Bram keeps his penny and James's silver stays where it is.

## Player's note: Session 1, James Worgen

**What worked**

- **The world felt lived-in and independent.** Dov's patter, Hobb's tally stick, Bram's pride, Ned's terms ("the rag goes straight across this table, I never close my fingers on it"), Widow Tallow counting spoons. Every NPC had a voice and wanted something of their own. Bram refusing to sell his penny on a failed Persuasion was a good failure. It came from who he is, not from punishing me.
- **The curse was shown, not explained.** The bootlace, the pie, the ale, the penny rolling uphill, then the crock, the stair tread, the pack strap, the shutter. It escalated physically and I always knew it was the coins. The Coin of Tymora working as a cold compass was a great, quiet way to give my patron a presence without a voice from the sky.
- **The cat** was the best thing in the session. Its smell-and-picture messages ("Lye. Wet linen. Tired.", "I keep away," said unhappily about the linen) gave it a personality. The 100 ft link limit was honoured, and I liked feeling it thin out.
- **Failures moved the story.** The botched switch became the owning-up scene, which led to Ned, which led to the coppers changing hands. Nothing stalled.
- **The nat 20 on Pim's palm** (the line going slack, the click of a coin on a table somewhere) was the high point. It earned the Inspiration.
- **Clues layered well.** Ned's copper not silver, then Tam Gorrey, then the sergeant's chalk crosses, then Wren's Rivington list, then Tallow's beeswax and "never gold", then the coin leaning at the curtain. I always had a next step without being railroaded.

**What broke or confused me**

- **Roll cards.** On the Religion and Sleight of Hand pair I had to press [Roll the die] several times. The already-resolved Religion card kept reappearing, and the reroll flow was hard to follow. The follow-up note "here are both tries in order" restated what the narration had already said.

If it can, give me the button.

**What was missing**

James keeps his eyes off the barrel and the three cards. That takes more effort than it should. He drops a hand to scratch the cat between the ears, and without speaking aloud he sends it a thought: *Stay with me. Tell me if whatever's over there moves.*

When the man ahead clears the table, he steps up and sets his regimental pay slip on the trestle so the Tethyrian seal faces her.

"James Worgen. Late of Queen Zaranda's foot, and after that whoever was paying." He nods at the cat. "That one's with me. He doesn't pay tolls, and he doesn't take advice."

turns.reply:
James keeps his eyes on the trestle. The cards are still slapping down behind him, *find the lady, friends*, and he doesn't look. Under his fingers the cat's ears flatten for a moment, then come back up. It doesn't move from his boot.

The answer comes the way the cat's answers always come, more feeling than words: *Still there. Not moving. Watching the barrel-man. Not us.*

The sergeant glances at the pay slip, then looks at it properly. She turns it a little toward the lamp with one inky finger, and the Tethyrian seal catches the light.

"Zaranda's." She doesn't say it like a compliment, but she doesn't say it like an insult either. She chalks *WORGEN* onto the board in square capitals, then copies it into a thick ledger lying open by her elbow. Her pen moves along the page past the day's names. A few lines higher up, two or three names carry a small chalk cross in the margin, done in the same hand.

"Business, work," she says as she writes. She looks at the cat once, briefly. "The cat's not my problem till it bites someone. Walking's free. Carts pay."

She slides the pay slip back across the trestle.

"A bed. Inside the walls, the Elfsong. It's dear, but nobody wakes up short there. Out here—" she tips her head north along the span, toward the lamps and the dark bulk of Wyrm's Rock in the middle of the river "—Tallow's, last door before the Rock. A widow runs it. She bars the door at midnight and counts the spoons. Her prices will rob you. Nobody else will."

The chalk taps once against the board while she thinks about something.

"Honest work, the Fist is hiring. It pays late. But it pays."

Then she looks past his shoulder, at the barrel and the lean man's busy hands, and her mouth goes flat.

"And whatever you do in the Gate, don't win anything at that barrel." She has already turned to the family behind him. "Next. Name, and your business."

James leans on the lamp post and lets his shoulders drop like a man who has walked a long way and hasn't decided where to sleep. The cat leaves his boot without any fuss. It pads to the nearest stall, goes up a rain barrel and onto the low shingled roof, and is gone along the ridge line, just a darker shape against the dark.

That leaves James with the barrel.

The man in the waistcoat is good. He isn't great, but he's good, and on a bridge at dusk that's plenty. It's the old throw. He holds two cards in his right hand, one above the other, and lets one fall. Every eye on the barrel follows the top card down. Every time, the card that drops is the bottom one. His patter rides over it: *watch her, friend, watch the lady, she's shy*. The drovers follow the card they think they saw, and they lose a silver each, cheerfully, one after another. Nobody beats that throw by watching. You'd have to stop his hand.

Then he does something James doesn't expect.

A broad drover in a sheepskin puts down his silver. The waistcoat man slows down, only a hair. The lady's corner has a crimp in it, and for one pass he lets it show, the way a sharp gives a win to his shill so the crowd will play. But the drover isn't a shill. He's a stranger with dung on his boots, and he points straight at the lady and turns her over and whoops.

"There she is, there she is! You've got the eye, friend." The sharp gives back the silver stake. Then he doesn't go into the waistcoat pocket where the rest of the evening's silver went. He opens a second purse, small and greasy, tied apart on his left hip, and counts coppers out of it into the drover's palm. Ten of them. "Copper spends the same, friend, copper spends the same."

The drover grumbles about it, laughing, and pockets them. The sharp pulls the purse string tight and settles it back on his hip with a little pat, the way you'd check a knife you don't want to cut yourself on. The next man in loses two silver straight, and all of that goes into the waistcoat.

A thin boy in a too-big jacket has been hovering at the back of the drovers. He edges forward with a coin pinched in his fingers. The sharp doesn't even look up. "Not tonight, little friend. You've had yours this week." The boy hangs there a moment, then slides off into the crowd going south.

The cat's answer reaches James before the cat does, the way it always does: cold slate under its paws, then a picture behind his eyes.

*One. Man. Sitting on a crate in the gap, back to the wall. Grey coat, hood down. Young. Smells of ale and onions.* Then, sharper: *Steel. Short. Left side of his belt.* And then something the cat clearly finds odd: *He scratches a stick with the knife. Each time the barrel-man takes silver, a scratch. When the barrel-man paid, no scratch. He looked at the purse. Long look.*

The cat comes down the rain barrel and settles against James's boot again as if it had never gone. The drover in the sheepskin is shoving through toward the lamps, jingling his winnings, and as he passes the post every hair along the cat's spine stands up.

*Smell,* the cat sends, flat and urgent. *On him. Wet stone. Old candles. Wrong.* It watches the sheepskin coat go off north along the span until the crowd swallows it.

The man in the gap hasn't moved. The sharp has already started his patter for the next mark. The checkpoint queue shuffles forward, and nobody is looking at a tired traveller leaning on a lamp post.

James lets the patter fade behind him: *watch the lady, friend, she's shy*. The lamp post gives him up without fuss, and he's just another tired back with a pack on it, walking north where the sergeant pointed.

The cat goes up a drainpipe and is gone. A moment later the feeling of it comes back: tar-paper and wet shingles under its paws, the drop to the street on one side, and threaded through the bridge's smells of fish, smoke, horse and too many people, one cold line of *wet stone, old candles*, moving north at a walk.

Following him is easy. The drover isn't hiding from anyone. He's a big man in a big coat, pleased with himself, and he walks the way a countryman walks in a town, down the middle of the street, stopping to look at things. A handcart of turnips is going the same way. James drifts in behind it and lets its owner set the pace, about forty-five feet back. His boots make no sound on the stones. The houses lean in overhead. Upstairs a woman is shaking out a cloth from a window, someone is frying onions, and a child somewhere is being told off for the third time.

Halfway along the span the drover stops at a pie-man's brazier. He buys a hot mutton pie and pays with a silver bit from his own coat. The coppers stay where they are, and he gives the pocket a pat and a jingle as if they might be lonely. The pie-man makes change. The drover turns away with the pie in his fist and his mouth already open for it.

His bootlace snaps.

James sees it happen. The man puts his weight on his right foot, the boot slides half off his heel, and he goes down on one knee in the gutter. The pie lands face-first in something that came out of a horse. The drover kneels there and looks at it. Then he laughs, a big, rueful laugh, and the pie-man laughs with him and won't give him another for free. The drover gets up, wet to the knee, ties the broken lace in a fat knot, and goes on north with his boot flapping.

*Same smell,* the cat sends from somewhere above. *Stronger when he fell. Like a cellar door opened.* Then, uneasy, it adds: *Fur wants to go up. I don't let it.*

The drover doesn't go down to the water and doesn't meet anyone on the street. Near the north end of the span, where the bulk of Wyrm's Rock fills the sky and the houses give way to the old fortress wall, he ducks under a low lintel into a taproom built right out over the railing. A sign hangs by one chain: a painted fence rail and six copper pennies, *The Sixpenny Rail*. Through the open door come lamplight, pipe smoke, and the noise of a room full of drovers and carters. A cheer goes up for him, someone shouts *what happened to you, then?*, and he starts telling it.

Three doors further on, the last door before the Rock, a narrow house shows a single lit window and a brass plate polished to a shine. That's Tallow's. Its door is open for now, with midnight still hours off.

The cat settles on the Rail's roof ridge, right above the door, and tucks its paws under. *He sits. By the fire. Others round him. The smell stays with him.*

Nothing else on the street is paying any attention to James. The turnip cart rattles on toward the fortress gate without him.

They all succeeded as written: the drover never spotted James, he didn't turn off the bridge, go down to the water or meet anyone on the way, and the cat kept him in its nose all the way to the Sixpenny Rail.)*

The Sixpenny Rail is one long low room. Its back wall is the bridge railing itself, boarded in and shuttered against the river. There's a fire at one end and a plank bar at the other, and in between is a fug of pipe smoke, wet wool and boiled mutton. Somebody has hung a horse collar over the hearth for luck.

A stout woman with her sleeves pushed up looks at the silver, decides it's real, and sweeps it into her apron. A tankard of something brown arrives. They listen while he counts on his fingers: the lace, the pie, the ale, the penny that rolled uphill. One of them glances down at Bram's flapping boot. Another looks at the wet patch down the sheepskin.

The silver goes down on the table beside the copper, and Bram looks at the two coins side by side.

Bram looks at them for a long moment. He's no longer grinning, and nothing else in the room is moving either.

Then he reaches past the silver and picks the dark penny out of James's linen with his bare, thick fingers.

"No, friend." He doesn't say it angrily, but he says it firmly. "Forty head up the Way and none of 'em lame. I've been unlucky before. A lace is a lace and a pie's a pie, and I spilled my ale because I'm a great clumsy ox, ask anyone here." Somebody does laugh at that, but only a little. "I won her fair. If I sell her for a silver to the first quick-handed stranger who tells me she's cursed, then I didn't win her, did I? I just got paid to carry her up the bridge for you."

He pushes the silver back across the table with one finger and leaves it lying by James's hand. Then he flicks the bright Tethyrian penny after it. It spins, falls flat, king up.

He turns back to the fire and the corner closes round him. Someone starts on a story about a mule.

It isn't quite over, though. An old carter in a leather cap is sitting at the end of the bench, and he didn't laugh at any of it. He leans over to Bram without looking at James and speaks low. He isn't quite low enough.

"You spend them coppers before you sleep, Bram. Humour me." He sucks his pipe. "And keep off the quays while you're in the Gate. You've heard what the Fist keeps fishing out down there. Men with a coin in their teeth."

The mule ate a tinker's hat, then the tinker's lunch, and then, the carter swears by his mother's grave, the tinker's wedding ring. Bram laughs at every turn of it, but he doesn't slap his pocket again.

The cat's answer comes back through the roof beams: wind across the shingles, the smell of the river, a long empty street below. *Here. He sits. Nobody at the door.*

Then he raises his eyes and studies James the way a man studies a horse at a fair: legs first, then teeth. At last he nods at the stool.

He hears the questions out without interrupting, and he takes his time answering.

"Copper." He says it low, under the mule. "Sailors pay her in silver, when they pay at all. They throw it over the side going out. Nobody puts it in a dead man's mouth." He touches the porter but doesn't drink yet. "These are coppers, old dark ones. There's a corporal of the Fist drinks in here of a tenday. He's pulled three out himself. He told me that much."

"You picked that penny up with your sleeve. Not your fingers." It isn't an accusation, just something he noticed. "So either you know something, or you think you do."

He puts the pipe back between his teeth and speaks round it.

He doesn't take it straight away. He draws on his pipe and lets the smoke go up into the rafters.

"A lady." He looks once at the hand James laid on his chest and doesn't ask which one. "Thought it might be that."

He turns the porter a quarter turn and says his piece.

"Day after tomorrow. Haskett, his name is. Corporal Haskett. He stands the gate at the Rock and comes off at the late bell, and he's in here before it's done ringing. Sits there." He tips his head toward a stool by the shuttered back wall. "He'll drink your porter. He won't say much for it."

Then he puts one finger on the silver. He doesn't pick it up.

"I'll ask him. I won't carry them, mind. Not to the door, not past this bench." He means it as terms, not as an apology. "He tips them into a rag, the rag goes straight across this table into your hand, and I never close my fingers on it. That's the way of it, or it's no way."

He gets up stiffly, leaves his pipe smoking on the plank and takes the silver with him. Then he shoulders onto the bench beside Bram, right in the middle of the mule. He pulls the spotted neckerchief off his own neck, tips the coins into it and ties the corners in a fat knot, the same kind of knot he put in his bootlace. Ned's silver goes into the pocket the coppers came out of.

He stops at the end of the bench and holds the knot out over the plank.

*Someone. Girl. Came up from the bridge, fast, now slow. Stands under the sign.* There is a picture behind it: a thin shape in a shawl that is too big for her, looking up. *She looked at me. Then at the door. She knows me.* A pause while the cat sorts out a smell. *Lye. Wet linen. Tired. No grey coat. No wet stone.*

She looks up at the ridge first. Then at him.

"Keep your four silver, Wren. Buy your brother some boots that fit." He glances once at the river side of the bridge, where the lamplight runs out over the black water. "I'll be honest with you, because you came a long way to ask me straight. I don't know yet if it comes off. You threw his coppers in the river and he still fell, so whatever this is, it isn't only in the coins. That makes it worse, not better. But I've got ten of the same pennies in my pocket right now, and a lady at my back who doesn't care for this sort of thing. I'll do what I can."

He shifts the pack on his shoulder.

"I need to see him. Tonight, if you'll let me. Not tomorrow, after another stair gives way." He keeps his voice low and plain. "Where is he now? Home, or still out on the span? And does he have any of their coppers on him tonight, anything he won since Tuesday?"

He tips his head up toward the ridge.

*Come down,* he sends to the cat. *Walk with us, a few paces ahead. Keep your nose on the street. If you smell wet stone or old candles anywhere near the boy or where they live, tell me. And if anyone follows us off this bridge, tell me before you tell me anything else.*

He looks back at Wren.

"Lead the way. I'll stay a step behind you, so it doesn't look like a stranger's walking you home."
turns.reply:
Wren's chin stays up when he tells her to keep the silver, and for a moment she looks as if he's insulted her.

"It's not for boots." She pulls her hand back under the shawl. "You'll have it when he stops falling. Not before."

Then she answers what he asked, quickly, the way she does once she's started.

"Home. I sent him back after the barrel. He'd limped all the way up there on that knee, just to get turned off." She stops, then starts again, faster. "Since Tuesday. He says no. He's lying. He won at the bones two days back, I heard him tell the Farrow boy. He says he lost them. Pim doesn't lose things. He's been hiding them since I threw the others in the river."

She looks at the step he's left her, the gap between him and the street, and gives a short nod.

"Nobody looks at a washergirl going home. Walk where you like."

The cat comes down off the ridge the way it went up, by the rain barrel, and drops onto the stones without a sound. It doesn't go to Wren. It goes past her and trots ahead down the middle of the span with its tail up, and Wren watches it go with the first thing close to a smile he's seen on her.

*Street,* it sends. *Smoke. Fish. Her: lye. Nothing wrong.*

They walk back south through the last of the evening. The span is quieter than when he came up it. The pie-man is raking out his brazier and doesn't look up. Upstairs, a woman is calling two names over and over until a pair of small boys run past James's knees and in through a door, and she says something to them about their supper that makes them both go quiet. A dog sleeps on a doorstep with its chin on its paws. Somewhere a man is trying to play a pipe and keeps getting the same three notes wrong.

The barrel is still working at the south end, under its lamp. *Find the lady, friends.* Wren crosses to the far side of the street without breaking step and doesn't turn her head. The cat sends him a picture of the gap between the shuttered stalls: grey coat, crate, knife scraping on stick. *Same one. Watching the barrel. Not us.*

At the checkpoint the queue has thinned to a carter and a mule. Sergeant Marrow is chalking something. She glances up as James passes going the wrong way, back out of the Gate, a pace behind a washergirl in a wet shawl, and her chalk stops on the board. She doesn't say anything. After a moment it starts moving again.

Past the trestles, Wren turns off the road and goes down a flight of stone steps that runs along the first pier of the bridge to the water. The south bank opens out below. A row of tenements leans against the stonework, four storeys of patched timber, with lines of wet washing strung between their windows. Wide, worn steps run down into the black river, scrubbed pale by years of laundry, and a few lanterns hang off hooks over them. It smells of lye, river mud and somebody's fish stew.

"Washing-steps," Wren says, though he can see that for himself. She points with her chin at a door with a sheet nailed over its broken pane. "Tam's. Someone else's now."

Three steps from the bottom, the strap of James's pack parts.

There's no warning, no fraying he'd noticed. It just goes, with a soft snap at the buckle, and the pack slides off his shoulder and lands on the stone with the dull clank of a mess kit. Nothing spills, and nothing is broken. The leather has torn clean across, right where it was soundest. Under his shirt Tymora's coin is as cold as it has been since the Rail, and against his thigh the bundle in his pocket stays warm.

The cat has stopped dead on the bottom step, looking back at the pack. Its fur is lifted all along its spine.

Wren has stopped too. She looks at the strap, then at his left hip pocket, and doesn't say anything. Her face says she's seen this before.

Their door is the second from the end. The stair inside is steep and dark, and the fourth tread is missing, freshly snapped, with pale splinters standing up from the stringer. Wren steps over the gap without looking down. At the top, a door with a rag stuffed under it lets out a thin line of candlelight. Her hand stops on the latch for a moment before she opens it.

The room under the eaves is small and clean. There's a washtub, a line of drying shirts, one candle in a saucer, and a straw pallet against the chimney breast. A boy sits on it with his back to the warm bricks. It's the thin boy from the barrel, in the same jacket that's too big for him. His right knee is bound up in strips of rag, and his left hand is wrapped to the wrist.

When the door opens, his good hand goes under the blanket. It moves fast and guiltily, and comes back out empty.

The cat slips in past Wren's ankles and stops in the middle of the floor, fur up, looking straight at the pallet.

*Here,* it sends. *Under him. Wet stone. Old candles.*

Pim looks from his sister to the tall stranger in the doorway, then down at the cat, and his voice comes out higher than he wants it to.

"Wren. Who's he?"

James sets the broken pack down just inside the door. He doesn't come any further in. He crouches with his back against the doorframe so his head is lower than the boy's, and lets his hands hang loose over his knees.

"Evening, Pim. I'm James. That's my cat. He doesn't bite unless you're a sausage." He tips his head at the bandaged knee, then the wrapped hand. "Washing-steps and a dog, your sister says. And the stair. Rotten week."

He pats the pocket on his left hip, and the bundle inside chinks dully.

"I'll tell you a secret, since you've got one of your own under that blanket. I've got ten of the barrel-man's coppers in here. Won fair, near enough. I've had them an hour, and my pack strap just tore clean through on your steps outside. Strongest bit of leather on it." He shrugs, rueful. "So you're not clumsy, and you're not cursed for being bad. Somebody's been paying you in pennies that bite. They paid Bram the drover the same tonight. They paid Tam Gorrey."

He digs into his belt purse with his right hand and counts out coppers on the floorboards between them, bright ordinary Gate pennies and the king-faced Tethyrian one on top. He puts down a few more than any bones table would pay an eleven-year-old.

"Here's a fair trade, man to man. You're not out your winnings. You keep these, they're clean. The ones under you go in here." He pulls the last scrap of silk from his component pouch and lays it open on the floor. "Don't pick them up with your fingers. Tip them in off the blanket, or use your sleeve. Wren, help him if he needs it."

While he waits he closes his left hand round Tymora's coin through his shirt, paying attention to it the way he did at the Rail: whether it goes any colder when the blanket moves.

"And while you do it, tell me something." His voice stays easy, as if he's asking about the weather. "When they let you win, the barrel-man and the bones-man, did anyone ever tell you to come back? Or ask your name, or where you sleep? Did a young fellow in a grey coat ever talk to you?"

*To the cat, silently: Stay right there. Keep your nose on whatever's under him. If anything in this room besides those coins smells of wet stone, the blanket, his bandages, the stair, the boy himself, tell me.*
turns.reply:
James lets the pack down inside the door with a soft clank and crouches against the frame. The cat stays where it is, in the middle of the floor, with its fur up.

Pim watches the cat. At the word *sausage* one corner of his mouth twitches before he can stop it. Then James pats his pocket and the bundle chinks, and the boy's face shuts again.

"I'm not clumsy." His voice comes out high and he pulls it back down. "I'm *lucky*. I win every week. Ask anyone on the span." The good hand creeps toward the blanket and stops halfway. "The steps were wet. The dog was just a dog."

Then the coppers go down on the floorboards one at a time: seven bright Gate pennies with the king-faced Tethyrian on top. Pim stops arguing and counts them with his eyes, twice.

"That's more'n I won."

"He said keep them," Wren says from the washtub. She doesn't move to help yet.

Pim looks at his sister, then at the silk lying open on the boards. He looks at the cat last, still staring at his blanket, and something in him gives up the fight. He pulls his jacket sleeve down over his good hand, feels about under the blanket and tips three dark coppers off the edge of the pallet onto the silk. They don't ring when they land. They thud.

When the blanket moves, the coin under James's shirt goes past well-water cold. For a moment it aches against his breastbone like a bruise.

"That's all of them."

"It's not," Wren says.

"It *is*—"

Wren crosses the room in two steps, kneels and runs her red fingers along the seam of the straw tick where the stitching has been picked open. She doesn't touch what she finds. She wraps the end of her shawl round her hand, pulls out a fourth copper and drops it on the silk with the others. Pim goes scarlet to the ears and studies the chimney bricks very hard.

Wren folds the silk's corners over the four coins with the shawl still round her hand and twists them shut. She leaves the bundle on the floor in front of James and doesn't take it a step further than that.

Pim scoops up the clean pennies one-handed and holds them tight. He rubs his knee through the rags while he works out his answers, and he gives them grudgingly, the way a boy does when he's sold something and isn't sure he got the better of it.

"Dov never said nothing. Just *off you go, little friend*, and the pennies." He sniffs. "Teague said come back. Teague's the bones. He's got a fish-scale apron and one tooth here." He taps his own front tooth. "First time, he asked my name. Said the bones liked me. Said come Tenday-eve, Pim, every Tenday-eve." A pause. "He never asked where we sleep. Everyone knows where we sleep. It's the steps."

At the grey coat his nose wrinkles.

"That's Hobb. He's Guild. He doesn't talk to the likes of me." He shifts on the pallet. "He talks to Teague, though. Last Tenday-eve he had Teague by the apron behind the fish stalls, saying the table was *owing*. Teague said it wasn't his table. Hobb said he didn't care whose table it was." He looks up, a little proud. "Nobody saw. I saw."

Then, quieter, looking at his bandaged hand:

"I don't feel any different."

The cat's answer comes in under the boy's words. It's slow, as though it has been checking twice. *Under him: nothing now. Straw. Lye. Boy.* Then the fur along its spine lifts again a little. *On him, still. Faint. Not the coins. Him. Like the drover's coat after, but the drover's went away.* A last uneasy picture: the boy's thin wrists and the rag on his knee. *It stays.*

Wren is still kneeling by the pallet. She sees James's face change at whatever he's just heard, though she can't hear it herself, and her own face sets hard.

"You said it doesn't come off with the river." She doesn't plead. She lays it out flat. "So is it off him now, or isn't it?"

James picks up the little silk bundle with his cuff pulled over his fingers and puts it in the left hip pocket with the others. Then he answers Wren the way she asked, flat and straight.

"The coins are off him. Something else isn't. Not yet." He doesn't soften it. "The drover's went away once he gave his pennies up. Pim's has been on him longer. Since the harvest, you said." He looks at the boy. "So it's had time to settle in. That doesn't mean it stays."

He shifts on his heels so he's facing the pallet.

"Pim. I want to look at that knee and that hand. I won't hurt you." He holds up his palm. "And I'm going to do a small thing first. It'll feel warm. That's all it is."

He takes Tymora's coin out from under his shirt and lets it hang on its cord in the candlelight. He doesn't hand it over. Under his breath, too low for the boy to make out, he says the words he's said every morning since the last hand: *Lady, you put me on this road. Here's a boy who's been robbed of his luck. Let me see who robbed him.* Then he lets the Lady's light run out of his open hand, a soft gold glow over the rag on the knee and the wrap on the hand. It's a small mending, two dice of it and no more, enough to close a split and take the ache out of a bite.

While the light works, he watches. He wants to see where it takes easily and where it doesn't, whether some patch of skin stays grey under the gold or the coin goes cold when the glow touches a particular spot. When it's done he asks Wren to unwind the hand wrap, and he looks for anything that shouldn't be there: a bruise that's the wrong shape, a small dark mark like the one on the pennies, branched like a twig.

"And think hard for me, Pim," he says quietly. "Teague. Did he ever touch you? Shake your hand, ruffle your hair, put the bones in your palm himself? Did he give you anything that wasn't a penny?"

*To the cat: Tell me if the smell gets stronger or weaker while the light's on him. And where it's strongest.*

*(Out of game: Healing Light, bonus action, 2 dice of the 6 on Pim. Arcana or Religion to read the residue, whichever you think fits.)*
turns.reply:
James pulls his cuff down over his fingers and lifts the silk bundle off the floorboards. It's heavier than four coppers should be, and it doesn't clink. He tucks it into the left hip pocket beside Bram's neckerchief, and the warmth against his thigh doubles. The Coin of Tymora is hanging free on its cord now, out from under his shirt, and it swings a little and goes so cold the cord feels damp.

Wren hears him out without moving. *The coins are off him. Something else isn't.* Her mouth tightens at that. When he gets to *that doesn't mean it stays*, she lets out a breath through her nose and nods once, as if that's the most anyone has told her straight in months.

Pim doesn't like any of it.

"It doesn't hurt." He pulls the bandaged knee in toward himself. Then he sees the coin turning on its cord in the candlelight, worn gold with a woman's face on it, and he stops pulling. "Is that real gold?"

James says his words too low for the boy to catch, and opens his hand.

The light comes out of his palm soft and gold, like lamplight through honey. It settles over the rags on Pim's knee and the wrap on his hand, and Pim goes very still. Under the light the knee straightens on its own, the way a leg does when the hurt goes out of it. Pim stares at it. He flexes it once, then again, harder, and his face does something an eleven-year-old's face isn't supposed to show in front of strangers. The ache from the bite goes out of his shoulders. Seven measures of the Lady's mending are more than a boy that size needed. The split is closed and the bite is closed.

James is watching for more than the healing, and he finds it.

The light settles easily into the knee and the bitten hand. It does not settle into the boy's right hand, the good one lying open on the blanket. It slides off that palm the way water slides off wax, and leaves the skin there looking a shade greyer than the rest of him, like copper going green. As the glow passes over that hand, the Lady's coin stops swinging on its cord. It hangs crooked, tipped a finger's width off true. It isn't pointing at the boy. It points past him, at the shuttered window on the river side. Through the coin James feels the pull: a thin, steady draw, like a fishing line paid out from that palm, running out through the wall, down toward the water and then along it, further than he can follow. It's no stronger than a line with a small fish on it, and it doesn't slacken.

When the light fades, the coin swings true again.

*Weaker,* the cat sends from the middle of the floor. Its fur has come down a little. *Knee: gone. Bitten hand: gone. Good hand: stays. There. Only there.* The cat's nose points at the open right palm.

Wren unwinds the wrap on the left hand without being asked, and does it carefully. Underneath is an ordinary dog bite, an arc of tooth marks that are now pink and shut. There's no mark, nothing branched, nothing that shouldn't be there. Just a boy's hand that a dog had hold of three days ago.

Pim is still flexing the knee. Then he answers the question, distracted, still looking at his leg.

"Teague?" He thinks about it. "He never ruffled me. He's not like that." He lifts his right hand off the blanket and turns it over without seeming to know why he picked that one. "First time, he put the pennies in my hand himself. Pressed 'em in and shut my fingers over them, like this. *Hold tight, Pim, they're yours.* He did it every time after." His nose wrinkles. "Gave me a herring once. It was off."

Wren is looking at the right palm too. She has seen the grey, or she's seen where James was looking. She doesn't say anything. She sits back on her heels and folds her cracked hands in her lap, the way someone does when they have decided to keep them still.

 James lets the last of the glow die off his fingers. The Lady's light has done everything he asked of it. The split knee is knitted whole, the bite is shut, and the boy is sitting up straighter on the pallet than he has in days.

The reading worked too. James found what still clings to Pim: one cold, grey patch on the right palm, the hand Teague pressed the pennies into, and from it a thin line running out through the wall toward the river and on along it. He can feel it there under his attention, steady and taut, the way you feel a line that's still hooked on something you can't see.

James looks at that grey palm for a long moment. Teague pressed the pennies in and shut the boy's fingers over them. *Hold tight, Pim, they're yours.* What one hand can do, another can undo.

He lifts the cord over his head. He doesn't give the coin away; he keeps the cord wound twice round his own wrist. Then he holds out his hand, palm up, the way you'd offer to shake on a bargain.

"Pim. One more thing, and then I'll leave you be." He keeps his voice easy. "Give me that hand. The right one."

When the boy does, James lays Tymora's coin in the grey palm, worn face up, and folds Pim's fingers over it with his own. He keeps his hand closed round the boy's fist.

"Hold tight, Pim," he says. "This one's not yours. It's hers. She only lends it." Under his breath, for the Lady alone: *You won me back once when I'd staked everything. He staked nothing and lost anyway. Take back what's yours from whoever's pulling on him. Let the line go slack.*

He holds on and pays attention to everything at once: the cold of the coin in the boy's fist, whether it warms or bites, whether that thin line out through the wall toward the river shivers, slackens, or pulls back harder, and which way along the water it runs.

*To the cat: Watch his hand. Tell me if the smell goes, or moves. And if something on the other end of that line notices us, if anything comes up those stairs or onto those steps, tell me first.*

Without looking away from the boy's fist, he asks Wren quietly:

"When's Tenday-eve? How many nights from now?"
turns.reply:
James lifts the cord over his head and winds it twice round his own wrist. The worn gold swings once and settles. Pim watches it the way he watched the clean pennies on the floorboards.

When James holds out his hand, palm up, the boy doesn't move at first. He looks at his sister. Wren gives him a short nod from where she kneels, and he puts his right hand into James's, grey palm up and a little damp.

The coin goes in face up. James folds the thin fingers over it with his own and closes his hand round the boy's fist.

"Hold tight, Pim. This one's not yours. It's hers. She only lends it."

Under his breath, only for the Lady, he says the rest. Then he holds on and listens with everything he has.

The cold hits first. For a heartbeat the coin in the boy's fist is colder than it has been all night, a bite that goes up through James's knuckles into his wrist. Pim flinches and doesn't let go.

Then the line answers.

James feels the whole of it at once, clearer than under the healing light. It runs from the small fist out through the shuttered window and down the pier stones to the black water. There it turns and runs along the river. It doesn't cross to the city. It goes west, downstream, along this bank and under the lamps of the south shore, out past where he can follow. It's thin and taut and it's been taut for months.

And it goes slack.

It doesn't break. It slackens the way a line does when the hand at the far end loses its grip. The pull that ran out of the boy's palm runs back the way it came, down the pier, along the water and away west. At the very end of it, far off, there's a twitch, the jerk of a line when whatever is holding it feels the weight come off all at once. Then James can't feel it at all.

Inside Pim's fist the coin goes warm, warm as a hand that has been holding it a long time. Somewhere close, though nothing in the room has moved, there's the small flat click of a coin set down on a wooden table.

James opens his hand, then the boy's fingers. The palm under the worn gold is pink, an ordinary boy's palm with a washing-steps callus at the base of the thumb. There's no grey left on it.

*Gone,* the cat sends. Its fur has gone down flat along its spine, all at once. *Boy only. Straw, lye, boy.* After a pause it adds, *Stairs empty. Steps empty. Nothing comes.*

Pim stares at his own hand. "It's warm," he says, sounding almost offended. "It was cold and now it's warm."

Wren has heard the question. She doesn't answer it straight away. She's looking at her brother's open palm, and her jaw is working the way it did on the step of the Rail.

"Eight nights." Her voice is lower than usual. "He won at the bones two nights back, so eight more. Tenday-eve, after the fish stalls shut." She looks up at James. "He'll go. He always goes. Whatever you just did, Teague will put more in that hand and shut his fingers over them, same as always."

James takes the coin back gently, winds the cord off his wrist and drops it inside his shirt again. It's warm against his breastbone now, the first warmth since the barrel. He lets out a breath he didn't know he was holding.

"Thank you, Lady," he says quietly, and doesn't explain it to either of them.

He looks at Pim and lets the boy see he means it.

"Listen to me, Pim. You're lucky tonight because she says so, not because Teague does. So here's the bargain. You don't go near the bones on Tenday-eve. Not to watch, not to win, not to tell Teague you've stopped. If he asks after you, you've got a bad knee." He nods at the knee, which isn't bad any more. "And on Tenday-eve, I'll be at that table instead of you. If anyone presses a penny into a palm that night, it'll be mine."

Then he turns to Wren and keeps his voice low.

"You're right. It'll come back if he does. So he doesn't." He tips his head toward the shuttered window, the river side. "That line ran out of his hand, down to the water, and west. Downstream, along this bank, under the south shore lamps. A long way. Not across to the city. What's down there, Wren? Past the washing-steps, along the water on this side. Docks, warehouses, a shrine, anything somebody might keep cellars under. Wet stone and old candles."

*To the cat: Go out on the steps and sit where you can see the water and the stair door both. If anyone comes down from the bridge, or anything moves on the river that's not a boat going about its business, tell me.*

James takes the coin out of Pim's palm. Pim lets it go, though his fingers want to close on it again. James unwinds the cord from his wrist and drops the coin back inside his shirt. It's warm against his breastbone, the first warmth he's felt from it since the barrel.

"Thank you, Lady."

Wren hears it and doesn't ask. Pim looks at the ceiling as if the Lady might be up there in the eaves.

When James gives him the bargain, the boy's face works through several answers. He picks the worst one first.

"But that's my table." He sits forward on the pallet. "If I don't go, there's no pennies. Teague'll give my win to the Farrow boy. He's been after it since harvest." Then, quieter, he gets to the part that really matters to him. "Wren can't do the rent on washing. Not all of it."

"I can," Wren says flatly. "I did before."

*Going,* the cat sends, and it's off the washing-steps and up the stone flight to the bridge before he reaches the bottom. The pictures come quickly. *Steps: empty. Water: black, nothing.* Then the trestles. *Sergeant: still there. Board half rubbed out. Folding up.* Then the gap between the stalls, and it slows down. *Grey coat: not on the crate. At the barrel. Now same.* At the same moment, the cold side of the Lady's coin in James's fist gives one small tug. The pull is toward the yard first, and then past the yard, west, like a line twitched from very far away. Then it goes still. Nothing comes down the passage and nothing touches the shovel. *I stay,* the cat sends. He sleeps again, and this time he sleeps till morning.

He wakes rested, the whole way through. The night has given back everything the evening spent: the Lady's light is full in his hands again and his pact is fresh.

Breakfast is laid in a front room no bigger than a pantry. There's a heel of yesterday's loaf, a lump of hard cheese he didn't pay for and won't be charged for, and a jug of small beer. Widow Tallow is at the sideboard counting teaspoons into a drawer, one at a time, under her breath. A second lodger sits at the end of the table. He's a bald gnome with oil-blackened thumbs, eating very fast and reading a broadsheet folded down to the shipping notices. He nods at James once and doesn't say a word.

"The cat had the passage all night," Tallow says without turning round. "It didn't come near my linen." Nine, ten. She shuts the drawer. "I put out cheese. Don't make it a habit."

Outside, the span is a different street in daylight. The fish stalls are going up with a lot of shouting. Dov's barrel stands empty by the checkpoint with a wet sack thrown over it, and the gap between the shuttered stalls holds nothing but a crate. The trestle has a young Fist man behind it this morning, who yawns over his chalkboard. Somewhere behind James the cat is still at its post. As he walks south the feel of it thins out and goes, past the hundred feet his link will carry. It's a small, ordinary loneliness, and he's had it before.

A little short of the south end the houses lean in hardest. Up on the third storey of a chandler's, a woman throws her shutters open to the morning. They bang back against the wall. Under James's shirt the Lady's coin goes cold all at once, sharply enough to ache.

Then a hinge creaks overhead, a dry creak that keeps going, and the lower shutter tears off its pins and comes down.

James doesn't look up. He has spent years under falling things. His body hears that creak the way it used to hear a crossbow string let go, and he moves before he thinks: one long step sideways and half a turn, shoulder in toward the wall. The shutter comes down past him, close enough to stir his hair. It's four feet of oak with an iron bar across it. It hits the stones where his head was a breath ago and breaks in two, and one half skids across the street into a fishwife's empty basket. Above him the woman screams, then leans out and swears. James is standing against the chandler's wall without a mark on him, and the coin under his shirt is warming on its right side as fast as it went cold. For an instant there's a smell of something sweet, like spilled wine, gone before he can be sure of it.

"Lathander's *teeth*." The woman is already halfway down her stair and comes out wiping her hands. "Them pins was new at midsummer. My man put them in himself." She looks at the oak, then at James, then at the place he was standing. "You've the Lady's own feet, you have."

The fishwife has pulled her basket out from under the broken half and is examining it for damage, loudly.

South off the end of the bridge the Trade Way goes on toward Amn. Rivington turns off it to the west, along the bank, the way Wren counted it out on her fingers. First come the fish wharves. The smacks are in, gulls are screaming over the gutting tables, and a Calishite in a striped robe sits under an awning with a ledger and a strongbox and a queue of sailors. Then the smokehouses, low and black, with oak smoke rolling out of their louvres. Then the ropewalk, a covered shed so long that its far end goes grey with distance. Inside it men walk slowly backwards, each paying out hemp from a bundle at his waist while a boy turns the wheel. Beyond it the tanneries, which he smells long before he reaches them.

Ropewalk Lane runs down beside the shed toward the water. It's cobbled, steep, and busy at this hour. There's a net-mender with her nets hung on the wall, a cooper, a cookshop selling something fried in a twist of paper, and a woman carrying a kettle under her arm with the face of someone about to pawn it.

He finds Shrike's near the bottom, where Tallow said it would be. It's a narrow frontage squeezed between the net-mender and a chandler's yard, with a half-door whose top leaf stands open. There's a plain board over the lintel. It might have been painted once. Inside, about ten feet back, is a small counter with a brass scale on it. The man behind it is grey and neat, with spectacles on a cord and his sleeves held up with garters. He's weighing the woman's kettle, which got there before James did. Behind him is an inner doorway with a heavy brown curtain across it. Even from the street, over the fish and tar and the tannery reek, the curtain lets out a thread of beeswax smell. Good candles, a lot of them.

Below the shop the lane ends at the strand. The tide is out. On the wet shingle stands a squat black stone with a niche cut in it, crowded with candle stubs. A fishwife kneels there with her shawl over her head, putting something on the stone that catches the light. It's Umberlee's, with the river water still running off it.

Under James's shirt the Lady's coin is doing two things. Its cold side still points back the way he came, east, toward a coal hole on the bridge. And as he stands across the lane from that half-door, the coin hangs crooked against his chest. It's tipped a finger's width off true on its cord, the way it tipped in Pim's room. It isn't leaning toward the man at the scale, or toward the shrine. It leans toward the brown curtain.

The grey man gives the woman three coppers for her kettle, writes something in a book and hangs the kettle on a hook behind him. He hasn't looked into the street yet. It's a little before eight, and the lane is full enough that one man standing still in it isn't strange yet.

James doesn't stop across from the half-door. He keeps walking, as if the lane is just the way down to the water, and buys a twist of whatever the cookshop is frying for a copper. It turns out to be sprats. He leans on the cooper's wall a few doors up, where he can see Shrike's counter at an angle without staring into it.

He eats slowly, like a man killing time before a boat. With one hand he presses the Lady's coin flat under his shirt so its tilt doesn't show through the linen.

He watches for a few things. Who goes in, and whether anyone goes past the counter and through the brown curtain. What the grey man pays out, and whether any copper comes from a different drawer or purse than the rest. Whether he ever glances toward the strand.

When the sprats are gone he licks his fingers, drops the paper, and wanders on down to the bottom of the lane. He stops at the edge of the shingle, well short of the fishwife at the black stone so he doesn't disturb her. From there he turns and looks back up at the rear of the row: the backs of Shrike's, the net-mender's and the chandler's yard where they meet the strand. He's looking for cellar gratings, a door or steps at the waterline, a drain mouth, anything wet-stoned that the tide would cover twice a day. He keeps an eye on the coin's lean, to see whether it points at the curtain from the front or at something lower from down here.

He doesn't go near the shop door.

turns.reply:
James buys a twist of paper from the cookshop for a copper. The woman behind the fat-kettle scoops sprats into it with a slotted spoon, salts them without asking, and is already serving the next customer. They're hot, small and crisp, and better than they had any right to be at eight in the morning. He takes them up the lane to the cooper's wall, where a stack of new staves gives a man something to lean on, and from there he has Shrike's half-door at a slant: the counter, the brass scale, and the edge of the brown curtain.

Under his palm the Lady's coin lies flat against his chest and stays tilted, a finger's width off true, like a dog that has stopped walking with its nose pointed somewhere.

He eats one sprat at a time and watches the counter.

Most of it is a pawnbroker's ordinary morning. A sailor with a tarred pigtail pledges a sea-knife in a sheath and gets silver. A girl of about twelve brings a pewter christening cup wrapped in a stocking and leaves with a few coppers, holding them tight. The grey man writes each pledge in his book before he pays, every time, and pays out of a single drawer under the counter, silver and copper alike. James watches his hands the way he watched Dov's. There's no second purse and nothing from under the counter. No coin goes out that didn't come from the till. The one thing he does that a till-clerk wouldn't is weigh the coppers. He puts even three pennies on the brass scale, taps the pan once, and only then slides them across. Plenty of pawnbrokers do that, against clipped coin. Plenty don't bother.

Then a woman in a good shawl gone thin at the elbows puts something small on the counter. It catches the light: a ring. The grey man looks at it without picking it up and says something too quiet to carry. Her voice carries fine.

"It's *gold*. It's real gold, it was my mother's—"

He says something else just as quietly and pushes the ring back toward her with one finger. She snatches it up and comes out through the half-door red in the face. She passes close enough to the cooper's stack that James hears her mutter "Ashe's, then, Ashe's," as she climbs the lane.

Nobody goes past the counter, and nobody touches the brown curtain. It hangs still the whole time, letting out its thread of beeswax.

The Rock's bell drifts over the rooftops from the bridge, marking eight. At the first stroke the grey man takes his spectacles off. He polishes them on their cord without looking at them, and he looks out through the half-door, down the lane, toward the strand and the water. It isn't a glance. He holds it a beat too long, the way a man looks at a sky he expects weather from. He isn't looking up the lane at the cooper's wall. Then the spectacles go back on and he bends to his book.

James finishes the last sprat, licks salt off his fingers, drops the paper and wanders down the lane like a man whose boat is late.

At the bottom the cobbles give out onto shingle, grey and wet, scattered with weed the tide left behind. The fishwife is still on her knees at the black stone. He stops a good way short of her and turns his back to the river to look up at the row.

From down here the houses show their other face. The fronts on the lane are timber and plaster. Their backs stand on old stone, a sea wall of big dressed blocks much older than anything built on top of it, stained dark green up to a hard line about head-high where the tide reaches twice a day. The net-mender's has a little slipway of planks running down to the shingle. The chandler's yard has a water gate, a squat timber door in the stone with iron straps on it, its bottom edge rotted ragged by the tide. Between them is Shrike's: blank stone with no door and no steps. A single small window is set in the footing just above the green line, barred, with a shutter closed behind the bars.

Under his hand the Lady's coin has changed its lean. At the half-door it pointed level through the shop at the curtain. Down here it tips upward and inward, at the rear of Shrike's and that window, or the room behind it.

He looks harder at the stonework round it.

He looks for a long minute and the stone tells him nothing more. It's wet blocks and green slime, with sea-wrack caught in the bars. The shutter behind them is shut flush, and the morning glare off the wet shingle flattens everything to the same dull shine. There might be a drain somewhere along the footing, or some mark that would mean something to a man who knew where to look, but James can't find it. All he knows is that there's a window just above the tide line, and that the Lady's coin is pointing at it.

Behind him the shingle crunches. The fishwife has finished at the stone and is getting up stiffly, one hand on her knee. She pulls her shawl back off her hair. She's a broad woman of fifty with forearms scaled to the elbow in fish-silver. On her way past she looks him over, a stranger staring up at the back of a pawnshop, and decides he's harmless.

"If you've a man out, she takes silver." She jerks her chin at the black stone, where a new coin sits in the niche among the candle stubs, bright against the wet. "Copper's an insult. Mine went out on the *Gull* at four." She doesn't wait for an answer. She goes off up the lane with her empty basket on her hip, calling something rude to the cooper, who calls something rude back.

The tide is still well out. The lane behind him is filling up with the morning, and the grey man is at his scale.

 He gives the footing one last careful look from the drain line up to the green, and comes away with nothing. His eyes slide over the wet blocks without catching on anything, and whatever else is down there behind Shrike's, he doesn't find it this morning. He knows only the window, the bars, the shut shutter, and the way the Lady's coin points at it.
