## Player's note: Session 1, James Worgen

**What worked**

- **The world felt lived-in and independent.** Dov's patter, Hobb's tally stick, Bram's pride, Ned's terms ("the rag goes straight across this table, I never close my fingers on it"), Widow Tallow counting spoons. Every NPC had a voice and wanted something of their own. Bram refusing to sell his penny on a failed Persuasion was a good failure. It came from who he is, not from punishing me.
- **The curse was shown, not explained.** The bootlace, the pie, the ale, the penny rolling uphill, then the crock, the stair tread, the pack strap, the shutter. It escalated physically and I always knew it was the coins. The Coin of Tymora working as a cold compass was a great, quiet way to give my patron a presence without a voice from the sky.
- **The cat** was the best thing in the session. Its smell-and-picture messages ("Lye. Wet linen. Tired.", "I keep away," said unhappily about the linen) gave it a personality. The 100 ft link limit was honoured, and I liked feeling it thin out.
- **Failures moved the story.** The botched switch became the owning-up scene, which led to Ned, which led to the coppers changing hands. Nothing stalled.
- **The nat 20 on Pim's palm** (the line going slack, the click of a coin on a table somewhere) was the high point. It earned the Inspiration.
- **Clues layered well.** Ned's copper not silver, then Tam Gorrey, then the sergeant's chalk crosses, then Wren's Rivington list, then Tallow's beeswax and "never gold", then the coin leaning at the curtain. I always had a next step without being railroaded.

**What broke or confused me**

- **Roll cards.** On the Religion and Sleight of Hand pair I had to press [Roll the die] several times. The already-resolved Religion card kept reappearing, and the reroll flow was hard to follow. The follow-up note "here are both tries in order" restated what the narration had already said.
- **Spending Inspiration.** I held Heroic Inspiration from the nat 20 but never saw a button to spend it. I only saw "allowed reroll" buttons, and the save cards said "No reroll on this card: its damage is already dealt" before I'd even rolled. If Inspiration can't be used on those, say so. If it can, give me the button.
- **A correction for something I didn't say.** The note claimed "the tin isn't stolen. Wren lent it to you," but I never said it was stolen.
- **Bookkeeping noise:**
  - An empty `<ledger></ledger>` tag leaked into the text.
  - "Wren receives 4 silver… she already had them" is clutter.
  - My starting 350 gold showed up as 315 gp / 315 sp / 350 cp, which doesn't match the campaign file.
- **Sheet inconsistencies:**
  - The rapier is +5 in the item text but +2 in the records.
  - Healing Light is "up to 5 dice" in the files but "up to 4" in the records.
  - "Seven measures of the Lady's mending" read as seven dice when it was 2d6 = 7.
- **Unintroduced name.** Sergeant "Marrow" appeared by name though she never gave it.
- **Odd travel times.** Bridge to Ropewalk Lane took 1h50, then the shrine at the bottom of the same lane took another 30 minutes.

**What was missing**

- **Variety in the curse threats.** Four Dex saves against falling objects in a row started to feel samey. One social or omen-type consequence would have broken the pattern.
- **A clearer ending.** The session ended mid-scene on a failed Perception with no wrap-up, no recap of open threads (Haskett in two nights, Wren on fifth day, Tenday-eve in eight nights, the tin in the coal hole), and no hook to leave on.
- **Passive Perception.** On the stonework, a quick read off the score before calling for a check would have been nice.
- **The cards.** Tymora's ban came up only in passing. I expected the temptation to bite harder at the barrel, and I'd welcome that.

Overall: a strong, atmospheric opening I want to keep playing. Most of the rough edges are interface and ledger, not story.

after.text:
Yes, a few. The biggest one first.

**The barrel, right at the start.** I wanted to sit down at Dov's barrel. Not to win. I'd watched him do the drop-the-bottom-card throw, and James is proficient with cards. I wanted to put a silver down, catch his wrist mid-throw, turn over the card he was palming and say "that's not the lady, friend" in front of the drovers. It would have been the most James thing to do all night: an old card-man calling out a sharp.

I didn't because of Tymora's ban. I wasn't sure whether exposing a cheat counted as playing, and I didn't want to break the pact in the first ten minutes over a guess. So James kept his eyes off the cards and I played it safe. Looking back, I wish I'd asked out of game: "?Does calling out a cheat at the table break the ban?" That's exactly the kind of temptation the sheet says the DM can use. I think the scene would have been better if I'd walked into it and let the DM decide the cost.

**Following Hobb on the way back.** When the cat showed me Dov counting silver into Hobb's palm with neither of them looking round, I badly wanted to peel off and tail Hobb instead of going to bed. I didn't because I'd just finished a long scene, the curse was dropping stairs on me, and I was carrying the tin. Leading whatever that is toward a Guild man felt reckless. It was the right call, but it's the thread I most regret leaving.

**Sending the cat behind the curtain at Shrike's.** On Ropewalk Lane the obvious move was to slip the cat in through the half-door, under the counter and past the brown curtain. I couldn't, because I'd left it guarding the coal hole on the bridge, well out of range. That was my own choice, and a fair consequence, but standing on the strand failing a Perception check I really felt its absence. Next time I'll think harder about where the cat sleeps.

**Two smaller ones:**
- At the checkpoint I wanted to ask the sergeant about the chalk crosses beside some names in her ledger. I didn't because she'd already turned to the next family, and James wasn't going to push a Fist sergeant on his first night.
- After Bram turned down my offer, I thought about rerolling the Persuasion, or using Friends on him. I didn't. Charming a man out of the thing he said he was keeping on principle felt wrong. I'm glad I didn't, because Ned's deal was better than anything magic would have given me.

opening.text:
The Trade Way ends in noise. Carts grind onto the stones of Wyrm's Crossing, porters shout over each other, and somewhere above the river a bell marks the evening. Lamps are being lit one by one along the bridge. Houses and shopfronts lean over the span, so the crossing feels less like a road and more like a narrow, crowded street hanging over the Chionthar.

The queue at the checkpoint shuffles forward. A family with bundles on their backs passes the trestle table; a carter argues about a toll and loses. Behind the table, a Flaming Fist sergeant with ink on her fingers and a chipped red gauntlet rubs her eyes and writes on a chalkboard without looking up much.

A few paces off the line, a lean man in a too-good waistcoat has turned a barrel into a table. Three cards flick under his hands, face down, face up, face down. "Find the lady, friends, find the lady! Long road, short game, a silver says you've still got your eye!" A couple of waiting drovers lean in to watch. The cards slap down again, crisp and familiar.

At James's feet, the cat has stopped. Its tail is up and its ears are turned, not toward the cards, but somewhere along the bridge, where the lamplight thins between two shuttered stalls.

The man in front of James steps up to the table. The sergeant's chalk taps the board.

"Next after this one — name, and your business in the Gate."
